senses: Any of several small trees having leaves that are white and downy underneath.
ety: English, used in mid-16th century; variant of whiting.

senses: Having a backbone.
Of, being, or pertaining to Vertebrata, animals with backbones.
ety: Adapted borrowing of French vertébré, from Latin vertebrātus (“jointed”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

senses: Someone who seeks to revive something.
An evangelistic preacher.
examples: And in 1975 one of the hottest Austin ensembles was the posthippie western swing revivalist group known as Asleep at the Wheel.
Lynton & Barnstaple Railway revivalists have unexpectedly been given a second chance to purchase the station, after the original sale deal fell through.

senses: Not metered, not charged on a meter (as Internet bandwidth).
A sudden stoppage of work.
A similar mass action of people leaving a place as a form of protest.
examples: Many people agreed this play did not belong in the festival: this tied with House on Mayhem Street for most walkouts, and was the subject of much angry discussion afterwards.

senses: A similar fold in a filter, lampshade, or various other products.
ety: From Middle English, from a variant of plait, from Old French pleit. Doublet of plait.

senses: A dish of braised or stewed sauerkraut or cabbage, with bacon, mushroom and onion or garlic.
Cabbage soup.
ety: From Polish kapusta, Russian капу́ста (kapústa), Slovak kapusta, Ukrainian капу́ста (kapústa).
examples: Fresh kiełbasa is made, center cut pork chops are trimmed just right, and the kapusta (sauerkraut) is prepared for cooking.
Then the kapusta was packed into jars super tight and topped with a little kraut juice.
And there would be the typical mother/daughter bickering over how much salt to add to the kapusta, a traditional cooked cabbage dish.

senses: The art of performing a difficult task so gracefully that it looks effortless; calculated nonchalance.
ety: Borrowed from Italian sprezzatura (“nonchalance”), which was coined by Baldassare Castiglione in 1528. The term gained currency in English in the mid-20th century, often to describe art.
examples: In men's fashion the ultimate style move is sprezzatura, embracing intentional errors such as undone buttons and misaligned neckties. Gianni Agnelli, the head of Fiat, wore watches over his shirtsleeves.

senses: A gold, silver or electrum coin of ancient Greece.
ety: From Latin statēr, from Ancient Greek στατήρ (statḗr).

senses: An extremely dedicated fan (enthusiast).
examples: Baseball has its superstars, pro football has created a superbowl, and college football is stuck with the superfans.
Now, finally, there’s growing agreement about his obvious unfitness. Indeed, some former Trump superfans are suddenly wondering if he might be the Antichrist.

senses: The process of indenting.
An empty space at the beginning of a line to signal the start of a new paragraph.
A fisherman.
A fishing boat with identical bow and stern.
ety: After the apostle Peter, a fisherman.

senses: A cordial syrup made from pomegranates.
A dilute drink made from this syrup.
A thin gauzy fabric of silk or wool, used for women's clothing and men's woven luxury ties.
A dyestuff consisting essentially of impure fuchsine.
ety: Borrowed from French grenadine, from Middle French grenade (“pomegranate”).

senses: Resembling or characteristic of milt.
A small (typically pork) sausage, usually served fried.
ety: Borrowed from German Bratwurst. The word is partly from braten (“to fry”) + Wurst (“sausage”), and partly from an older Middle High German brātwurst, in which brāt is an unrelated word meaning “ground meat” (compare German Brät). In modern German, the term Bratwurst is used almost exclusively for sausages fried or to be fried.
examples: Yesterday we had bratwurst for dinner.

senses: The soft inner part of something, especially the pith of a fruit.
ety: Borrowed from Latin medulla (“pith, marrow”), perhaps from medius (“middle”).

senses: One who pickles food products.
A cucumber grown for pickling.
A machine that pickles metal.
examples: The slicing cucumbers' production systems are geared to be first on the market, whereas for the picklers this urgency is not so great.

senses: A piece of thin patterned cotton or linen fabric used like a bathrobe in Mediterranean countries, originally Tunisia.
Having vacuoles
A monumental tower, usually ornate, at the entrance of a temple, especially in Southern India.
ety: From Tamil கோபுரம் (kōpuram), Malayalam ഗോപുരം (gōpuraṁ), from Sanskrit गोपुर (gó-pura).

senses: Of tea, having a large amount of tips, or leaf buds.
ety: 1790, tip (“apex”) + -y (diminutive). Sense of “clever” may be influenced by tip (“inside information”).

senses: A crew member of a warplane; airman.
An aircraft formerly operated by the military, but now owned privately.
Any aircraft decorated in military livery for display at airshows etc.
A heavily-armed starship.
Exterior to a synapse.
A tar-like substance formed at high altitudes on stony mountains and used in traditional medicine.
That is involved in, or aids collaboration; collaborative
A person or device that determines a schedule, that determines the order that tasks are to be done.
Any technology concerned with the nervous system.
A plant, Foeniculum vulgare, of the parsley family, which has a sweet, anise-like flavor.
The bulb, leaves, or stalks of the plant, eaten as a vegetable.
The seeds of the fennel plant used as a spice in cooking.
ety: From the Middle English fenel, from the late Old English finuðl, finule (weak feminine forms); fenol, finul (masculine forms), from Proto-West Germanic *fenukl, from the Vulgar Latin *fēnuclum, fēnoclum, from Late Latin fēnuculum, from the Classical Latin faeniculum, a diminutive form of faenum (“hay”); compare the Italian finocchio, the Occitan fenolh, the French fenouil, and the Spanish hinojo. Doublet of finocchio and finook.

senses: Something that quenches (thirst, fire, etc.)
ety: From Middle English quenchere, equivalent to quench + -er.

senses: An oligomer having eight subunits.
A large external pipe in a water-tube boiler, carrying unheated water from the steam drum down to the water drum as part of the circulation path.
A pipe for leading the hot gases from the top of a blast furnace downward to the regenerators, boilers, etc.
The quality or state of being pusillanimous; the vice of being timid and cowardly, and thus not living up to one's full potential; pusillanimousness.
ety: From pusillanim(ous) + -ity, from Middle French pusillanimité, from the ecclesiastical Latin pusillanimis, from pusillus (puny) + animus (spirit) + -ous. A translation of the Greek ὀλιγόψυχος (oligópsukhos, “faint-hearted”).

senses: Of, related to, or composed of integuments.
A round Spanish cap, with flaps at the back or sides, once used by hunters.
A person who forgives.
examples: Take second best, put me to the test. / Things off your chest you’d need to confess. / I will deliver, you know I’m a forgiver.

senses: A piece of wood, etc., laid between the cords and boards of a book to flatten before cutting.
ety: From Middle English trindel (“wheel, roller”), from Old English tryndel (“circle, ring”), from Proto-West Germanic *trundil (“ring, hoop”), equivalent to trend + -le. Akin to Low German tründeln (“to roll”). More at trend.

senses: An imitation of the Mohawk hairstyle in which a central tuft is created using gel without having to shave the sides of the head.
One octave higher; as a marking, typically abbreviated 8va.
ety: From Italian ottava (“octave”) (also feminine form of ottavo (“eighth”), ordinal form of otto).

senses: A state of fullness, a great quantity (of something).
A legislative meeting (especially of the Communist Party) in which all members are present.
An enclosed space having greater than atmospheric pressure.
The space above a false ceiling used for cables, ducts etc.
ety: From Latin plēnum n (“space filled with matter”), from plēnus (“full”). The sense of "legislative meeting" is a semantic loan from Russian пле́нум (plénum, “plenary session”), from the same Latin source.

senses: Removal from a superior place in a hierarchy.
